title: The Next Evolution of Trend Following ft. Nick Baltas - Systematic Investor - Ep.410

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The Next Evolution of Trend Following ft. Nick Baltas - Systematic Investor - Ep.410.docx

speakers: Nick Baltas (systematic quant strategist at a large investment bank)
summary: Systematic Investor Ep.410 (July 2026): trend and carry performance in 2026, AI in research, Graham paper on market universe size, Run One River defence framework, and thematic/narrative momentum papers.

coverage.note: intro, Die with Zero book, banter
AI model turnover, concert; AI in firms
AI use in research, hallucinations, morning agent
coffee, June/July CTA trend recovery and weak signals
2026 performance, carry and reversion, V shape in March
index numbers, Graham paper on universe size intro
Run One River Perfect Hedge paper

quant investing pillars and risk models

completeness_estimate: 0.70 - first reader captured the two main papers (Graham universe size, Run One River defence layers), the thematic/narrative arguments and the performance narrative accurately; missed the July month-to-date index numbers, client-demand comments, five-of-seven-months record, portable-alpha leverage logic (two points), the third-bucket specification, narrative life cycle and lead-lag mechanism, theme transience in covariance, the price-as-objective and price-path-as-proxy discussion, and Niels's sector-grouping scepticism

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the quote unquote best model at the moment get replaced like every 10 I think it was every 10 days or every 19 days
claims.claim: The frontier AI model changes every few weeks (versus months last year), making firm-level AI integration and tool choice hard; using a version one step behind captures most of the benefit.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: The primary use at least in my view and the things that we do we see on the day-to-day is more to enhance research
claims.claim: AI is mainly used for research (collecting, synthesising information, coding) with human in the loop; open-ended factual queries can be confidently wrong, so outputs require expert checking.
claims.conditions: Closed-form tasks easier to verify than open questions

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: build a little agent that goes out every morning before I wake up and I've given it certain things to collect for me like performance of the main CTA indices
claims.claim: A simple AI agent can collect CTA index performance and top stories each morning and flag relevant research papers, though numbers are sometimes wrong when websites lag.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we had a weak June as as as an industry. We had a soft start to July. Now things seems to be turning around in the last week or so for CTAs and trend followers.
claims.claim: In 2026 June was weak and early July soft for CTAs, then trend recovered led by energies, currencies and fixed income, with only some markets in each sector participating (a trend-pickers market).

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: some of the models that actually try to put a threshold on how aggressive they would be with weak signals have been lagging a bit behind
claims.claim: Models that limit position size on weak signals lagged in a rates sell-off because a small short is lucky only without strong signals; strong profit came from rates shorts and commodities.
claims.conditions: July 2026

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: Kerry has been very very strong both in the effect space and as you would imagine the commodity space with the backoration we're seeing
claims.claim: In 2026 carry was strong in FX and commodities (backwardation from geopolitical activity), complementing trend, and reversion had a strong four or five months, so the diversified multi-strategy aggregation worked.
claims.indicator: carry returns in FX and commodities
claims.direction: long carry in commodities with backwardation
claims.conditions: 2026 geopolitical backdrop

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: the typical Vshapes you know the the one per year so we had one this year right in March.
claims.claim: A V-shaped equity move occurs about once a year (March 2026), but this one was a fast recovery instead of a fast drop, so it hurt trend less; dynamic volatility scaling added value.
claims.conditions: V-shape with fast recovery

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: beta 50 is up 1.34% in July up 10% so far this year CT index up 0.89% 89% in July, up 10.37% for the year.
claims.claim: CTA indices were about +10% YTD at end of July 2026 against MSCI World +9% and the aggregate bond index -0.12% YTD.
claims.indicator: SG CTA Index; SG Trend Index; BTOP50
claims.conditions: Data to 22 July 2026

correction.issue: The index figures were read 'as of Wednesday' (the recording was on a Friday, upload date 26 July 2026), so they are to about 22 July, not end of July; July was a partial month, and Niels also gave July month-to-date figures that the claim omits.
correction.fix: As of the Wednesday before the Friday recording (about 22 July 2026) the Beta 50 index was about +10% YTD (+1.34% in July), the SG CTA index +10.37% YTD (+0.89% in July), the SG Trend index +10.15% YTD (+0.94% in July) and the short-term traders index +4.52% YTD; MSCI World was +9% YTD and the US aggregate bond index -0.12% YTD.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: high level long-term positive returns and some downside protection, some crisis alpha.
claims.claim: A trend follower delivers long-term returns and crisis alpha; if crisis alpha is the aim, use a small core universe because principal components (equity, duration) dominate in downturns, while for long-term performance add more diversifying markets.
claims.direction: small core for defence; broad for returns
claims.conditions: Crisis alpha driven by equity and duration

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: as soon as you cross 70 to 80 markets, the less liquid markets do not really add much in terms of performance.
claims.claim: Graham Capital finds beyond 70-80 liquid markets, adding less liquid macro markets (currencies, EM equities, swaps) adds little, but exotic commodities, including Chinese ones, still add return up to more than 100 markets, with a liquidity hump.
claims.conditions: Commodity diversification only

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: we typically operate between the 50 and the 100.
claims.claim: A practical universe is 50-100 markets; going broader costs capacity or adds nothing because adding same-factor markets splits a fixed risk budget.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: The first responders and that's like more like
claims.claim: A defensive portfolio has three layers: option-based hedges as first responders (reactive, costly), trend following as second responder for multi-month crises, and a diversifying third bucket (e.g. alternative risk premia) that moderates carry cost.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: it cannot be a short gamma exposure
claims.claim: The diversifying third bucket cannot be short gamma, because financing a hedge with downside risk turns the overlay into a relative-value trade rather than a defence.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if we made the trend following side more responsive, i.e. shorter term, it will be a better hedge.
claims.claim: Shorter-term trend may hedge a few days better but costs more in the long run and has become worse over the last decade; slower can be better.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: enhancing equities with a trend follower. I think it should come from the perspective of perhaps reduced upside participation in the trend program.
claims.claim: In portable alpha, trend on top of equities should limit its long-equity participation to avoid doubling risk on the upside.
claims.direction: cap long equity in trend overlay
claims.conditions: Equity-only portfolio

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: The equity bond portfolio is not facing its worst challenge when equities are falling. It is when both are falling.
claims.claim: For an equity-bond portfolio the main shock is inflation, when both fall, which unfolds over a quarter or more; unconstrained medium-term trend is the hedge for that.
claims.conditions: Inflation shocks

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: lowrisk stocks are typically coming with a greater than expected uh sharp ratio uh primarily
claims.claim: Low beta earns excess risk-adjusted return because leverage-constrained investors with benchmarks overbid high-beta names; systematic returns come from risk premium or structural/behavioral inefficiency.
claims.conditions: Leverage constraints

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: Risk factors are not always risk premier. risk factors explain risk.
claims.claim: Risk model factors (such as countries) explain risk but are not necessarily rewarded; risk models reduce dimensionality.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: themes are nothing more than a tagging operation.
claims.claim: A theme is just a tag grouping assets with a common feature; as investors allocate by theme, correlations within it rise beyond sector links.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: if the market is not elastic enough, it starts building some some some short-term price dislocation.
claims.claim: Theme allocation creates price pressure and short-term dislocation that momentum signals pick up, so thematic hype contributes to trends.
claims.conditions: Inelastic market

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: theatics in my mind is another way of of of of reducing dimensionality
claims.claim: Themes are another dimensionality-reduction layer with both risk implications (covariance structure) and potential dynamic allocation returns, even without a clear risk premium (like a stagflation narrative), akin to a trend-following mindset of intertemporal demand.
claims.conditions: No long-term premium implied

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: account for those then our prediction of portfolio risk is biased downwards sorry it's biased upwards
claims.claim: Ignoring thematic clusters in the covariance matrix biases risk estimates and misallocates risk; a theme-aware risk model (Lee) is better and applies beyond stocks to cross-asset trend portfolios.
claims.conditions: Theme associations are short-lived

correction.issue: The direction of the bias is omitted. Baltas says that if thematic clusters are ignored the predicted portfolio risk is biased (he says downwards, then corrects himself to upwards), concluding that the portfolio is riskier than the model suggests. Read with 'we're more risky than what we should have been', this means the risk model understates actual risk.
correction.fix: If thematic clusters are left out of the covariance matrix, the risk model understates the portfolio's true risk and misdistributes risk across positions (Baltas misspeaks on the direction but concludes the portfolio is riskier than reported); a theme-aware risk model (the Lee paper, tested on stocks) corrects this and the idea extends to cross-asset trend portfolios.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: the stocks that happen to have higher exposure on naratives that are becoming more popular outperform those that have less exposure to narratives that are fading.
claims.claim: Narrative momentum: stocks exposed to rising narratives outperform those exposed to fading ones, a signal distinct from price momentum that could enhance allocation models.
claims.direction: long stocks exposed to rising narratives; short those tied to fading ones
claims.conditions: Narratives rise, peak and fade over months

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: they take the 13.3 million articles and they they and they structure that into 347 narratives.
claims.claim: The narrative-momentum paper builds point-in-time data from 13.3 million articles since about 2013 into 347 narratives, with robustness checks on narrative definitions.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: We can make the argument that narratives are also correlated.
claims.claim: Look-ahead in narrative backtests is analogous to the factor zoo; using 30-60 evergreen topics (trade wars, stagflation, capex) reduces the problem since new themes correlate with them.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: and there is too much dimensionality.
claims.claim: Themes help discretionary investors reduce dimensionality because attention is limited.

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: we have been trained without it and we can assess the output and we have the wisdom or maybe the experience or the expertise to call the bluff from the truth
claims.claim: AI output is checkable today because current practitioners were trained without AI and can spot errors; Baltas worries about how later cohorts will keep that judgement if everything becomes a prompt, and Niels adds that without expertise supervision the output can run uncontrolled, so human expertise stays the control layer.
claims.conditions: Holds while models still make plausible errors; may change as models improve
claims.testable: no - qualitative judgement about skills and oversight

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: there is certainly increased interest you know across all fronts
claims.claim: Client demand for trend and diversifiers is rising across the board, driven by recent performance and protection data points and by trend being seen as a defensive trade; Baltas adds that institutions are becoming more focused on protecting the downside, which is why defence frameworks keep being published.
claims.indicator: client interest / allocations to trend following and diversifiers
claims.direction: inflows to trend and diversifiers up
claims.conditions: July 2026, after weak equity spells and geopolitical risk
claims.testable: partly - CTA fund flows can be measured, interest cannot

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: that's the seven month of the year right that's the fifth out of seven um assuming it closes positive
claims.claim: In 2026 Baltas's trend programs were positive in five of seven months (if July closed positive); the two losing months were June (reversion primarily in equities) and March (the V-shaped equity move), so the year's losses came from equity reversals.
claims.direction: trend positive most months, losses in equity reversals
claims.conditions: One bank's trend programs, to late July 2026
claims.testable: yes - monthly returns of trend indices

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: US aggregate bond index down 96 basis points and down 12 basis point now for the year
claims.claim: In July 2026 (to the Wednesday before recording) trend and CTA indices were up about 0.9-1.3% while both MSCI World (-0.84%) and the US aggregate bond index (-0.96%) fell, an example of trend gaining when equities and bonds fall together, which is the main equity-bond shock; the short-term traders index was slightly down.
claims.indicator: Beta 50 +1.34%, SG CTA +0.89%, SG Trend +0.94%, MSCI World -0.84%, US Agg -0.96% (July 2026 month-to-date)
claims.direction: trend positive when equities and bonds both fall
claims.conditions: Partial month; a rates sell-off helped short positions

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: flat to negative correlation to equity markets. Obviously not convex but certainly not concave either.
claims.claim: Specification for the third defensive bucket: flat-to-negative correlation to equities and a payoff that is neither convex nor concave (for example alternative risk premia), so it can offset the bleed of the first two layers without adding downside risk.
claims.indicator: correlation to equities; payoff convexity of the diversifying sleeve
claims.conditions: A short-gamma sleeve fails the test (see C08-2)
claims.testable: yes - correlation and convexity of candidate sleeves can be measured

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: They have different speeds for trend followers and they show which year which speed has done better.
claims.claim: The Run One River report tabulates by year which trend model, which speed and which structure (an integrated trend program versus a portfolio of asset-class trends) did best, implying leadership rotates between years, so a speed or structure should not be chosen from one year's ranking.
claims.indicator: annual ranking of trend speeds and trend constructions
claims.conditions: Baltas describes the content only; the conclusion about rotation is an inference
claims.testable: yes - rank speeds and structures per year in a trend universe

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the kind of extra leverage you're adding is quote unquote the trend which historically at least we can't talk about the future historically has been negatively correlated uh when your uh equities have gone into a longer crisis
claims.claim: In portable alpha, the notional leverage from a trend overlay is less risky than it looks, because the added exposure has historically been negatively correlated to equities in longer equity crises, so it works as a hedge rather than extra risk.
claims.indicator: correlation of trend to equities in prolonged equity drawdowns
claims.conditions: Historical pattern; fails if trend is long equities into a fast reversal

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: it's not that the increased leverage is creating the concern here it's the increased leverage on the asset that you're highly concentrated
claims.claim: Leverage itself is not the problem with stacking trend on a portfolio; the danger is added leverage on the asset the portfolio is already concentrated in, so for an equity-only portfolio moderate the long-equity risk of the overlay, while for equity-bond portfolios keep trend unconstrained.
claims.indicator: overlap between overlay exposure and core portfolio concentration
claims.direction: limit overlay's long exposure to the core asset
claims.conditions: Depends on the main shock the investor fears (equities down versus equities and bonds down)
claims.testable: partly - compare overlay variants in equity-only versus equity-bond portfolios

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: AI and the use of the machine learning and AI models has become now you know very very common um in pretty much all the topics we had
claims.claim: At the Goldman-hosted research conference machine learning, nonlinear models and LLM-based sentiment and thematic mapping appeared in almost every topic (portfolio construction, equity forecasting), showing AI/ML tools are now standard in financial economics research.
claims.conditions: Anecdote from one conference

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: there has been a bit of transition in the investment thesis um more around thematics
claims.claim: Since COVID investment theses have shifted toward themes (the stay-at-home theme being one example), with banks building thematic baskets that hedge funds use for active bets or hedges; this flow into themes is a driver of the rising within-theme correlation.
claims.conditions: Post-2020 regime
claims.testable: partly - thematic ETF/basket growth is measurable

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: thematic association is short-lived
claims.claim: Theme-driven clusters are transient, so a covariance matrix that captures them has to be updated dynamically to reflect how risk is distributed tomorrow, not just historical correlations.
claims.indicator: dynamic covariance estimation with thematic factors
claims.conditions: Applies to cross-asset trend portfolios as well as stocks
claims.testable: yes - compare static versus theme-aware covariance forecasts

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: They come they stay and they fade and through that cycle of popularity picking up at some point hitting the peak and then starts dropping
claims.claim: Narratives have a life cycle (rise, peak, fade) rather than appearing and vanishing overnight, so an asset's exposure to a rising narrative is persistent enough to be measured as a beta and to predict returns over the short term.
claims.indicator: narrative popularity trend; asset beta to narrative strength
claims.direction: long exposure to rising narratives, short fading ones
claims.conditions: Needs point-in-time narrative data
claims.testable: yes - narrative momentum paper provides a framework

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: there is a reason why price momentum exists. So if you go a few months back before price momentum was there there is an underlying engine that is creating excess demand
claims.claim: Narrative or fundamental demand precedes price momentum: an underlying engine creates excess demand before the price trend appears, so narrative exposure could be an earlier signal than price. Economic-trend models likewise treat the underlying trend as latent and use several proxies (past price path, economic regime, thematic exposure).
claims.indicator: narrative exposure as a lead signal for price momentum
claims.conditions: Speculative mechanism; lead-lag has to be tested
claims.testable: yes - lead-lag between narrative exposure and subsequent price momentum

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the beauty about price is that it's uh it's objective. It's recorded.
claims.claim: Price data is objective and recorded for decades, which makes trend research easy to test; thematic strategies lack an equivalent, since themes appear and vanish and it is unclear what the underlying data is or how to back-test them without look-ahead.
claims.conditions: Baltas answers with point-in-time article data and evergreen topics (see C15-1, C16-1)
claims.testable: no - statement about research data quality

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you're not going to be completely wrong by putting healthare companies together and just say yeah this is healthare
claims.claim: Sceptical view: simple sector grouping captures most of the clustering that thematic work tries to model, and thematic investing may partly be a way for Wall Street to get investors excited, since energy or healthcare companies already react similarly.
claims.conditions: Baltas replies that themes add information when they cut across sectors (for example memory chips within the AI theme)
claims.testable: yes - compare risk models with and without thematic factors beyond sectors

claims.speaker: Nick Baltas
claims.quote: itself is not necessarily the best predictor but it's an easily observable easily calculated and empirically validated
claims.claim: The price path is not necessarily the best predictor of the underlying signal, only the most observable and validated one; the macro regime, the price path and thematics are different transformations of the same underlying signal (denoising the truth), and in a prolonged growth regime they all point the same way (buy equities) and correlate.
claims.indicator: price trend versus macro regime versus thematic exposure as signals
claims.conditions: Signals agree in a prolonged growth regime and diverge at turning points
claims.testable: yes - compare signal combinations out of sample
